sections.h2: What should a seller know about Wilson, NC?
sections.html:
Wilson is a small eastern North Carolina city with affordable housing, a renter and owner split close to even, and a history built on a railroad and a tobacco market. The Census Bureau estimates 49,572 residents as of July 1, 2025, up 2.3% from the 2020 base, across 31.03 square miles of land.

Sellers here tend to be heirs, landlords, owners of older houses in the historic neighborhoods, or people leaving town. A listing can work well when the house is in good order. A direct sale to an investor or cash buyer can make more sense when the house needs repairs, has back taxes, or is tied up in a family estate.

  • Check the tax bill and any delinquent notice before choosing a route.
  • Find out whether the house sits inside one of the city's local historic districts.
  • Compare the net proceeds from a listing, after repairs and time on the market, against an as-is offer.

sections.h2: What do Census numbers say about Wilson housing?
sections.html:
Wilson is an affordable market. The 2020-2024 figures show a median owner-occupied home value of $210,700, median gross rent of $971 and an owner-occupied rate of 49.1%, so about half of homes are rented.

The city has 20,403 households averaging 2.31 people. The Census Bureau lists median household income at $52,485 and 23.0% of residents in poverty in the 2020-2024 data. Roughly 18.1% of residents are 65 or older, which fits the number of long-held homes that come to market through estates.

sections.h2: How did Wilson grow, and how does that shape its houses?
sections.html:
Wilson grew up around a railroad stop. The city's history page says the Wilmington and Raleigh Railroad reached the site in mid-1839 and named its station Toisnot, and the town of Wilson was incorporated on January 29, 1849. The first market sale of tobacco in Wilson took place on September 2, 1890, and tobacco acreage rose quickly afterward.

The housing that came from that boom is still visible. The city's historic preservation page describes the Old Wilson district, with 361 properties from the 1850s through the 1920s and a large collection of bungalows built in the 1910s and 1920s. It also lists West Nash, with 99 properties along a nine-block street, and Broad-Kenan, with 280 properties of which more than 60% are bungalows.

Many of these houses are now a century old. Original wiring, plaster, small closets and settled foundations are common, which affects financing and inspection results. A buyer who wants to restore the home may value that history. A buyer who needs a loan may not.

sections.h2: Do Wilson's historic districts limit what you can change before selling?
sections.html:
They can. The city has three local historic districts, Old Wilson, West Nash and Broad-Kenan, covering about 740 parcels under the jurisdiction of its Historic Preservation Commission. Two National Register districts, East Wilson and Central Business/Tobacco Warehouse, are not part of the local district and are not under the commission's authority.

  • Look up your parcel before you replace windows, siding or porches.
  • Ask the city's planning and community revitalization office what approvals apply to exterior work.
  • Tell prospective buyers early if the home is inside a local district, since they will want to know about future restrictions.

Stopping a project midway and listing the house unfinished is often easier than starting new exterior work in a district. A cash buyer takes the property as it is and handles approvals later.

sections.h2: How does Wilson County handle property tax?
sections.html:
Wilson County's Tax Administration bills real and personal property for the county and for the City of Wilson. The county reports about 43,000 parcels in its listing system, collects for 9 municipalities, 15 fire districts, two solid waste taxes and two special districts, and notes that Wilson County covers some 373 square miles.

Tax comes due September 1. The county says bills were mailed in August after the 2024 revaluation, and that taxes become delinquent after the January deadline, which the county's page gives as January 6. State law lets owners pay at face value if they pay before January 6, with interest after. Ask the office to confirm the exact last day for the year of your sale.

The office is at 2816 Ward Blvd in Wilson and answers at 252-399-2900. It treats postmarks as proof of timely mailing, and it warns that mail dropped at a local post office may not get a same-day postmark, so mail early or ask for a hand-stamp.

sections.h2: What did Wilson County's revaluation change?
sections.html:
The 2024 revaluation was the first reappraisal of Wilson properties since 2016, covering more than 41,000 real property parcels as of January 1, 2024. The county hired an outside appraisal firm and published a Schedule of Values, the rulebook for appraising every property during the next cycle. State law requires a reappraisal at least every eighth year, and the county says it is on an eight-year cycle.

The county reports that the deadline to appeal the new values ended May 16, 2024, when the Board of Equalization and Review adjourned, and the next chance to appeal real property values opened in January 2025. A real property bill is based on the value and owner on January 1, so a sale later in the year does not change who receives the bill. Assessments between reappraisals do not follow market swings, only new construction, demolition or damage.

  • Use the county's online comparison tool to see sales of homes in your area.
  • Appeal in the year you receive a notice, not after the board has adjourned.
  • A later appeal goes to the Property Tax Commission within 30 days of the board's mailed decision.

sections.h2: What happens if Wilson County property tax goes unpaid?
sections.html:
Collection can start immediately once a bill is delinquent. The county's delinquent real estate tax page lists garnishment of wages, attachment of bank accounts, rental income or income tax refunds, sheriff seizure of personal property, and foreclosure of real estate. The first foreclosure step is a newspaper advertisement of the delinquent account about two months after the bill goes delinquent, and costs and fees are added.

North Carolina law attaches the tax lien as of the listing date, and the lien is enforced by an action like a mortgage foreclosure in the county where the property lies. If you are behind, ask the tax collector about the exact balance before you sign a contract, since a buyer will need the lien cleared at closing.

Disabled veterans, elderly owners and disabled owners may qualify for relief. The elderly or disabled exclusion takes off the greater of $25,000 or half the appraised value, and the county's page prints the 2026 income limit as $38,800. The disabled veteran exclusion covers up to the first $45,000. The circuit breaker limits tax to 4% of income, or 5% in the higher band up to $58,200, and defers the difference. File with the tax office by June 1.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Wilson house that needs major repairs?
faqs.a: Yes. A cash buyer can purchase it as-is, and a traditional buyer may offer less to cover repairs. Houses in the historic districts date from the 1850s through the 1920s per the city, so ask for an inspection early.

faqs.q: Do I need approval to change a house in a Wilson historic district?
faqs.a: Possibly. About 740 parcels in the Old Wilson, West Nash and Broad-Kenan districts fall under the Historic Preservation Commission. Ask the city's planning office about your parcel before starting exterior work.

faqs.q: When is Wilson County property tax due?
faqs.a: It is due September 1 each year. The county lists January 6 as the last payment day, and state law allows payment at face value before January 6. Confirm the exact date with the tax office for your tax year.

faqs.q: I sold in the spring. Why did I get a tax bill?
faqs.a: Wilson County bills the owner of record on January 1, so a bill can reach a seller after a sale. Settle the share of the year's tax at closing and ask your attorney to confirm who pays the bill.

faqs.q: Where do I ask about relief programs in Wilson?
faqs.a: Contact the Wilson County Tax Administration at 252-399-2900, option 6, for homestead, disabled veteran and circuit breaker applications. Filing is due to the office by June 1 each year.
